text: Bones in Space. On Earth, your skeleton works hard every second of the day, even when you are just standing in line at the canteen. Gravity pulls your body towards the ground, so your bones must hold up your weight with every step. This constant load sends a signal to special cells inside your bones, telling them to keep building fresh, strong bone. On a space station, however, astronauts float, so their legs, hips and spine have almost no weight to carry. Without that load, the bone-building cells receive no signal and slow down, while other cells keep breaking old bone down at the usual rate. As a result, an astronaut can lose around one per cent of the bone in their hips and legs every month. The lost minerals travel into the blood, which is also why some astronauts develop painful kidney stones. Exercise machines that make astronauts push against heavy springs can slow this loss, because they create some of the load that gravity normally provides. Astronauts also eat foods rich in calcium and vitamin D, which their bodies need to build new bone. Even so, after returning to Earth, it can take years for their bones to fully recover.
